title: The petition
hook: here the one praying says why this Ardas is being made

segments.voice: Yesterday: maan, and your line: strength of the weak. Today, right after naming God that way, the Ardas finally says what it's for.

Sunday at the gurdwara. The congregation stands, hands joined, and the person leading the Ardas has been speaking for several minutes: the Gurus, the martyrs, the Khalsa, the gurdwaras far away, the honor of the humble. Then the voice changes slightly. A name is spoken, a family's name, perhaps. A new baby. A grandfather's surgery next week. A shop opening on Main Street. A student leaving for college. For a few seconds, a prayer that belongs to a whole people becomes about one household's Tuesday.
screen: `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.` → `A FAMILY'S NAME IS SPOKEN.` → `ONE HOUSEHOLD'S TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: This is the petition, the part of the Ardas where the reason is named. Everything before it is fixed and shared: the opening invokes the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib, then come the remembrances, the requests for the Khalsa and for the Sikhs, the line about maan. Then the one leading says something like: in Your presence, this Ardas is made for, and the reason is named in plain words. The congregation listens and joins the waheguru that follows. Some readers trace the word ardas to a Persian word for a written petition, the kind a person would hand up to a ruler's court. Whatever the root, the picture fits. A petition isn't a speech. It's short, it's specific, and it names what is being asked. And notice who can be named. Not only the person leading. A family can ask the granthi to include their purpose: thanks for a safe journey, a new job, the anniversary of a death, a child's exam. At home, a person praying alone names their own reason the same way. Nothing in the prayer asks for the reason to be grand, only plain. There's something steadying in that. The big, shared prayer holds a whole people's history, and inside it, your small reason is given a place, said out loud, in front of the Guru. Nobody is too small to have their reason named. And the prayer doesn't stop at one household: before it ends, it turns back out toward everyone.
screen: `THE FIXED PRAYER COMES FIRST.` · `THEN THE REASON IS NAMED.` · `ARDAS: A PETITION TO A COURT.` · `SHORT, HONEST, SPECIFIC.` · then, large: `SAY WHY.`

segments.voice: Let today's real concern rise, not the one you think you should have, but the one that's actually there: a worry, a hope, a thank-you. Put it into one plain sentence, no flourishes: this is for my mother's appointment, or, this is thanks for the week. If you pray, say that sentence quietly to the One; if not, just let it sit in the open.
The petition. The moment in the Ardas when the reason for this prayer is named in plain words, inside a prayer that belongs to everyone.
Your line: say why. A short, honest reason, said in front of the Guru. Day six hundred thirty-three, done.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, a family can ask the granthi to name their purpose in the Ardas, a birth, a journey, a remembrance; at home, the person praying names their own reason at the same point.

chat.says: Can a family's own reason, like a new job, really be named in the Ardas?
options: Yes: after the shared opening, the petition names the reason in plain words, even a small one.
No: only the shared, fixed words are said; personal reasons are kept silent.
Yes, but only big public events, like festivals, may be named before the Guru.
chat.meaning: In the petition, the one leading names the reason plainly: a new baby, a safe journey, an exam. Nobody is too small to have their reason named.
